sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Bureaucratic Authoritarianism**: Early nationalists fiercely criticized the **Indian Civil Service (ICS)** as an alien, highly paid, and unaccountable bureaucracy that monopolized key administrative posts.
• **Separation of Powers**: A foundational demand was the complete **separation of judicial and executive functions**, as district collectors simultaneously acted as judges and prosecutors, leading to systemic miscarriage of justice.
• **Police & Prison Reforms**: Nationalists exposed police brutality, torture of under-trials, and the high-handedness of the **provincial police forces**, demanding better recruitment and public accountability.
• **Local Self-Government**: Critique of the **Official Secrets Act** and reactionary measures under Lord Curzon that sought to officialize municipal bodies and curtail local autonomy.

items.term: Separation of Judicial and Executive Functions
items.definition: The primary administrative demand of the INC to prevent executive interference in judicial rulings, enshrined later in Article 50 of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
Nationalist demand to replace expensive British officials with qualified Indians to reduce administrative drain and ensure responsive governance.
The persistent demand by Moderates to hold ICS examinations concurrently in London and India to give equitable opportunities to Indian candidates.
Official bodies examining public services in India; nationalist members dissented against racial discrimination and inadequate representation of Indians.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Presidency Capitals (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras)**: Epicenters of intellectual debate, press memorials, and INC resolutions on administrative restructuring.
• **Imperial Legislative Council**: Platform where nationalist leaders like G.K. Gokhale and Surendranath Banerjee moved sharp resolutions on financial and administrative waste.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Stiff resistance from the Anglo-Indian bureaucracy, racial arrogance, and tokenistic reforms (like the Morley-Minto reforms which ignored administrative democratization).
• **Policy Interventions**: Continuous public petitions, press campaigns in newspapers like *Kesari*, *The Hindu*, and *Bengalee*, establishing precedents for modern Indian public administration.

items.title: Mnemonic for Moderate Administrative Demands
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "J-P-C-S" (Judicial, Police, Civil Services, Self-Government)
• **Decoded Meaning**: Judicial-executive separation, Police torture removal, Civil service Indianization, Local self-government expansion.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly eliminates incorrect options claiming Moderates demanded immediate violent overthrow rather than systemic administrative checks.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Moderates fought for 'Reform, Representation, and Reduction' (Reform of bureaucracy, Representation in governance, Reduction in military/civil expenditure).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that Moderates ignored administrative reforms and focused solely on constitutional reforms. This is false; administrative reforms like the separation of the judiciary and police accountability were central pillars of Moderate petitions.

Mains Value Addition: Connect the early nationalist demands for police and judicial reforms to contemporary Second Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) reports and Article 50 of the Indian Constitution to fetch top marks in GS-2 and GS-1.

keyTakeaways: The campaign for general administrative reforms formed the backbone of Moderate constitutional agitation between 1905 and 1917.
Key demands centered on judicial-executive separation, Indianization of civil services, and ending police brutality.
These historical critiques laid the ideological foundation for modern Indian public administration and constitutional safeguards like DPSP Article 50.
